title: Children of immortal bliss
hookLine: an Upanishad line read out in Chicago: hear, children of immortal bliss, and the atman it points to
carry: every soul is holy at the root

cards: Hear, children of immortal bliss. That's an old line from the Upanishads, and some days after his greeting, Vivekananda read it out to the same hall in Chicago. Not ladies and gentlemen.
Not friends. Not even sisters and brothers this time. Children of immortal bliss: every person in the room, named for what he believed they already were.
Today, his longer talk, the one printed as his paper on Hinduism.

teach.h: A SEER CALLS OUT TO EVERYONE.
teach.b: The line comes from the Shvetashvatara Upanishad, where a seer calls out to all the children of the immortal and says, in effect: I have known the great one, shining like the sun, beyond the darkness, and only by knowing that does anyone pass beyond death.
Vivekananda turns that call toward his listeners. They are not, at bottom, weak or fallen creatures, he tells them. He calls them children of God, sharers of immortal bliss, and holy.
The soul, in the Vedanta he describes, was never born and never dies; body and mind change, but what you are underneath does not.

teach.h: THE ATMAN: HOLY AT THE ROOT.
teach.b: Hindus call that self the atman, and this is one of Hinduism's biggest teachings: at the root, every person is divine. Then a second move.
Religion, he says, is not finally about accepting a doctrine or agreeing with a creed. It's about realizing: being, and becoming.

In the Hindu view he lays out, the point is to see the divine directly, not just to hear about it. Images, rituals and scriptures are helps along the road, steps for different people at different places.
For the Hindu, he says, a person isn't traveling from error to truth, but from truth to truth, from a lower truth to a higher one. A lower step isn't an error; it's simply where someone stands.
So the paper holds two things together: a very high claim about every person in the room, and a very patient view of how people get there. Children of immortal bliss, still learning to walk.

how: Vivekananda's paper on Hinduism is read in Vedanta study circles, and the Upanishad's call to the children of immortal bliss is chanted and quoted in Hindu talks and gatherings.

games.q: you've got one line to describe every person in a packed hall of strangers. which do you choose?
games.why: Vivekananda borrowed the Upanishad's address, naming his listeners for what he believed they already were.

practice: Think of the name you call yourself in your worst moments, and notice it without arguing.

Then try the Upanishad's name instead, child of immortal bliss, silently on the out-breath a few times, noticing what part of you resists and what part leans in; you don't have to believe it to try it on.
If you pray, you can rest in a prayer you already know.
